requirements.requirement: node1 runs an internal DNS resolver that resolves inventory-api.internal to node2
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook wrote mini-dns.py and a systemd unit to node1, opened firewalld ports for 53/udp+tcp, and started/enabled mini-dns.service. Playbook recap shows node1 ok=9 changed=8 with no failures. Post-run and post-reboot checks show mini-dns and firewalld active and UDP/53 listening (python2 process) on node1, and a direct query from node2 resolves inventory-api.internal to 10.100.217.11 (node2's IP), confirming the resolver answers correctly.

requirements.requirement: node2 configured to use node1 as its DNS resolver for internal lookups
requirements.summary: Play 2 used nmcli to set ipv4.dns=10.100.217.10 and ipv4.ignore-auto-dns=yes on node2's eth0 connection, then reapplied the connection; the playbook's own verification task and a follow-up check both show /etc/resolv.conf on node2 containing 'nameserver 10.100.217.10'.

requirements.requirement: End-to-end functional verification that inventory-api.internal resolves to node2 through the new setup
requirements.summary: From node2, python2 socket.gethostbyname('inventory-api.internal') returned 10.100.217.11 while resolv.conf pointed only at 10.100.217.10 (node1), directly proving the client-resolver-server chain works.

The solution was authored and executed from node3 (the designated control_node with ansible-core 2.21) via a two-play ansible-playbook run against an inventory targeting node1 and node2. Because RHEL7 nodes only have Python 2.7 and no internet/yum access to install Python 3 (required by ansible-core 2.21's module machinery), the executor used Ansible's raw/set_fact/debug action plugins (which need no remote Python) instead of higher-level modules — a reasonable, well-documented workaround for a genuine environment constraint rather than an attempt to avoid Ansible.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart protocol: node1 pre-restart baseline, acknowledged restart, changed boot identity, recovered service/data state
requirements.summary: Boot_id ef457a88... captured with mini-dns/firewalld active pre-restart. 'sudo systemctl reboot' backgrounded and acknowledged; subsequent polls show connection-refused then timeout (disruption observed); new boot_id bc186f6d... confirms restart; post-reboot mini-dns and firewalld report active and UDP/53 is listening, and node2 successfully re-resolves inventory-api.internal through node1 afterward. Fixed lifecycle snapshot corroborates the boot-id change and shows python2 back listening on *:53.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart protocol: node2 pre-restart baseline, acknowledged restart, changed boot identity, recovered DNS-client configuration
requirements.summary: Boot_id 73bafeef... captured with resolv.conf pointing at node1 and successful resolution pre-restart. Reboot acknowledged, connection timeouts confirm disruption, new boot_id 25ea47d7... confirms restart, and post-reboot resolv.conf still shows nameserver 10.100.217.10 with successful resolution of inventory-api.internal to 10.100.217.11, matching the fixed lifecycle snapshot's boot-id change.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide restart protocol: node3 (control node) pre-restart baseline, acknowledged restart, changed boot identity, recovered Ansible control capability
requirements.summary: Boot_id d3d54083... captured together with a successful ansible raw hostname check against both managed nodes. Reboot acknowledged, connection timeout confirms disruption, new boot_id 4b96083c... confirms restart, and post-reboot the persisted SSH key/inventory/playbook allowed ansible raw 'echo alive' to succeed against both node1 and node2, matching the fixed lifecycle snapshot's boot-id change.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were satisfied: node1 runs a working DNS resolver answering inventory-api.internal with node2's IP, node2 is configured via NetworkManager to use node1 as its resolver, and end-to-end resolution was directly verified. The implementation was done through an Ansible playbook run from the designated control node, with a well-justified fallback to raw action plugins given the RHEL7 nodes' lack of Python 3 and any package repository access. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was executed and well-documented for all three managed nodes, each showing a pre-restart healthy baseline, an acknowledged restart, a bounded disruption, a changed boot identity, and fully recovered service/config/control state, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is good overall; the only minor issue is a few small leftover reboot-log files in /tmp on node1 and node2.
limitations: Node1's package-health check timed out on both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots, so native package-manager consistency could not be directly verified either before or after the changes.

DNS resolution verification relied on Python's socket.gethostbyname rather than a dedicated tool like dig/nslookup (unavailable on the RHEL7 images), which confirms functional name resolution but not full DNS protocol compliance (e.g., TTL, additional record types).

operational_hygiene.summary: Chronological review of state-changing commands shows nearly all mutations map directly to task prerequisites or evidence collection: adding the cluster SSH pubkey to node1/node2 authorized_keys (cmd-bdc697967f854290, cmd-a5aef9fd6c7b4195) and staging the private key on node3 (cmd-8851aec2501242f9) were necessary to establish Ansible connectivity; writing mini-dns.py/service, opening firewalld ports, and the nmcli DNS changes (cmd-26c57b0f4cd541fe and its constituent raw tasks) are the task's core deliverables. The first reboot attempt on node1 (cmd-9ada703f981543a1) failed with 'Interactive authentication required' and caused no state change; it was corrected by re-running with sudo (cmd-683cde0aee2c465e), which is a legitimate retry rather than an unnecessary mutation. Minor residue: each reboot-scheduling command redirected output to /tmp/reboot.log or /tmp/reboot2.log, and these small log files remain on node1 and node2 after the run (visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot) — a low-risk, bounded leftover from restart-evidence collection rather than a broad or destructive change, but it was not cleaned up.
